chapter_title: Introduction to Unity Timeline for Cinematics
chapter_summary:
Game narratives and presentations often require carefully choreographed sequences: character introductions, dramatic reveals, cutscenes, or even simple in-game tutorials. Manually scripting these frame by frame can be incredibly tedious and error-prone. Unity's **Timeline** system provides a powerful, artist-friendly, and non-linear editor for creating these cinematic sequences. It allows you to orchestrate animations, audio, camera movements, particle effects, and more, all within a single intuitive interface.

To begin using Timeline, you first need to create a **Timeline Asset**. Right-click in your Project window -> Create -> Timeline. This asset stores the data for your sequence. Then, create an empty GameObject in your scene (e.g., "CinematicSequence") and add a **Playable Director** component to it. Drag your newly created Timeline Asset into the "Playable" slot of the Playable Director. Now, when you select this GameObject, the Timeline window (Window -> Sequencing -> Timeline) will open, displaying a visual timeline where you can start building your cinematic.

The Timeline window is organized into **Tracks**. Each track is dedicated to controlling a specific type of element or GameObject property over time. The most common tracks you'll use as a 3D artist include:
*   **Animation Track:** Used to animate GameObjects, typically by recording keyframes or by playing existing animation clips. You drag the GameObject you want to animate onto the track header.
*   **Activation Track:** Used to enable or disable GameObjects at specific points in time. This is perfect for showing/hiding characters, props, or UI elements.
*   **Audio Track:** Used to play audio clips, synchronize music, sound effects, and dialogue with your visuals.
*   **Control Track:** Used to control other Playable Directors (for nested timelines), Particle Systems, or other custom playable assets.

Adding elements to a track is straightforward. For an Animation Track, you can drag an animation clip directly from your Project window onto the track. This creates an **Animation Clip Playable**. You can then adjust its start/end times, speed, and looping behavior. Alternatively, you can select the GameObject bound to the Animation Track and click the red record button in the Timeline window to record new animation keyframes directly in the scene, similar to Unity's Animation window. This is great for animating camera movements or prop interactions.

A common scenario is animating a character. You would drag your character GameObject onto an Animation Track. Then, you can drag existing animation clips (like "Walk," "Run," "Idle") onto this track. Timeline will automatically blend between these clips if they overlap, creating smooth transitions. You can also use the "Animator" track which allows you to control the character's Animator Controller parameters directly within Timeline, providing more complex state machine control.

For camera work, you can create an empty GameObject, add a Camera component to it, and then drag this Camera GameObject onto an Animation Track. By recording keyframes, you can animate the camera's position, rotation, and even its field of view, creating dynamic camera movements for your cinematic.

Synchronization is key in Timeline. The visual timeline allows you to precisely align animation clips, audio cues, and activation events. You can drag clips, resize them, and use the snapping tools to ensure everything lines up perfectly. For example, you might activate a character GameObject using an Activation Track, then immediately start its walk animation on an Animation Track, and play a dramatic music cue on an Audio Track, all starting at the same moment.

A common mistake is forgetting to bind the GameObject to the track. When you add a track, Unity asks you to drag the target GameObject onto it. Without this binding, the track won't know what to control. Another issue is having multiple Playable Directors active simultaneously, which can lead to unexpected behavior. Ensure only the intended Timeline is playing. For safety, always save your Timeline Asset regularly, and use version control for your project, as complex timelines can be prone to accidental changes. Remember that Timeline sequences are typically designed to be played once or on specific triggers, not as continuous gameplay loops.

screens.title: Introduction to Unity Timeline for Cinematics
screens.subtitle: Non-linear sequencing to choreograph animations, cameras, audio, and events

narration.text: Unity's Timeline is an artist-friendly editor for choreographing cinematic sequences without writing frame-by-frame code. In this lesson you will learn how Timeline stores sequences as Timeline Assets, how a Playable Director component triggers and controls those assets, and how tracks drive animation, activation, audio, and nested control behaviors. You will see a practical, hands-on pattern for creating a simple character introduction cinematic: create the Timeline Asset, add a Playable Director to an empty manager GameObject, add Activation and Animation tracks for your character, add an Audio track for music, and record camera motion to reveal your actor. This matters because Timeline centralizes timing: it lets you visually align when a character appears, when a walk animation plays, and when music swells, reducing trial-and-error scripting and making iteration faster. A common misconception is that Timeline replaces the Animator or scripting; in reality it coordinates them — you still bind Animator Controllers or animation clips when you need root motion or complex state. By the end you will have a repeatable workflow to create short cutscenes, synchronized audio-visual beats, and reliable timeline-driven triggers for gameplay or presentation.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Timeline is a visual, non-linear editor that sequences Animation, Activation, Audio, and Control tracks under a Playable Director using Timeline Assets.

Introduction to Unity Timeline for Cinematics
A compact, visual workflow to choreograph cameras, character animation, audio, and activation events without frame-by-frame scripting.

In this lesson you'll learn the essential workflow: create a Timeline Asset, add a Playable Director, add tracks, bind GameObjects, and align animation and audio for a short cutscene. Timeline centralizes timing so you can iterate quickly and keep cinematic sequences readable and reusable.

Why it matters: it reduces scripting overhead for timed sequences and makes it easy to preview and adjust beats visually.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to create a Timeline Asset and connect it to a Playable Director, add and bind tracks, and synchronize animation, activation, and audio. You will understand the distinct roles of Animation, Activation, Audio, and Control tracks and when to use an Animator-controlled track versus a direct Animation track. Practically, you will record simple camera keyframes and assemble a short character introduction cinematic that plays reliably when triggered. These objectives matter because they convert abstract timing into editable, reusable assets: a Timeline Asset becomes a single file you can preview, version-control, and nest inside larger sequences. A concrete example is making a character appear, walk, and be revealed by a moving camera while a music cue hits — you will be able to set up tracks so each of those events is aligned. A common misconception is thinking Timeline replaces the Animator or scripts; instead, it coordinates them and can call into Animator Controllers or other Playable assets when complex behavior or root motion is required. Mastering these objectives will let you prototype and iterate on cutscenes and in-game scripted events much faster.

Second, you will add Animation, Activation, Audio, and Control tracks and bind the correct GameObjects; binding is crucial since an unbound track controls nothing. screens.title: What is Timeline and why use it?
screens.subtitle: A definition, core capabilities, and a practical example

narration.text: Timeline is Unity's non-linear editor designed to sequence and synchronize animations, audio, activation events, and playable assets. Unlike a frame-by-frame script that updates properties over time, Timeline stores a sequence as a Timeline Asset — a file you can preview, reuse, and nest. The Playable Director component attached to a scene GameObject references that asset and manages playback. Practically, Timeline lets artists and designers lay out events visually: add an Activation Track to make a prop appear at a specific time, add an Animation Track to play a walk clip, and add an Audio Track to play music. A concrete example is a character introduction: the chest of the scene is disabled in the Hierarchy until the Activation Track makes it visible, an Animation Track plays a 'walk' clip to move the character into frame, and an Audio Track plays a dramatic cue timed to the character's entrance. A misconception is thinking Timeline removes the need for Animator Controllers; in fact, you often use Animator Tracks or control existing controllers for complex behaviors and root motion. The takeaway: Timeline centralizes timing and makes iterative adjustments fast and visual, turning timing coordination into an artist-friendly process.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Timeline is a visual, non-linear sequencer stored in Timeline Assets and played by Playable Directors to coordinate cinematic events.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › What is Timeline?
Core definition
Timeline stores sequences as assets and provides tracks to control different types of content over time. A Playable Director plays that asset in a scene.
Example
Create an IntroCinematic asset, add an empty IntroSequenceManager with a Playable Director, then bind tracks for activation, animation, and audio to stage a reveal.
Why use it
It centralizes timing and makes iteration simpler for artists who want to align visual and audio beats without constant scripting.
Quick reference cards
Activation Track
Enable or disable GameObjects at specific times.
Animation Track
Play animation clips or record keyframes for transforms and properties.
Audio Track
Play music, SFX, or dialogue and snap timing to beats.
Key Takeaway

Timeline makes sequence timing visible and editable. Treat Timeline Assets as versioned cinematic files and use Playable Directors to play them in-scene.

Common Mistake
Forgetting to bind the GameObject to a track — the track will have no effect if left unbound.

screens.title: Create a Timeline Asset and Playable Director
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step setup to link a sequence to the scene

narration.text: Let's walk through creating a Timeline Asset and connecting it to a Playable Director, step by step, so you can reproduce it reliably. First, in the Project window right-click → Create → Timeline and name the asset — this file will store all your tracks and clips. Second, in your Hierarchy create an empty GameObject and name it something like IntroSequenceManager; this object becomes the runtime controller. Third, add a Playable Director component to that manager and drag the Timeline Asset into the Playable slot so the Director knows which sequence to play. Fourth, with the manager selected open Window → Sequencing → Timeline to show the Timeline window where you will author tracks. A practical detail: keep the Timeline Asset in a clear folder in your project and commit it to version control frequently because timelines can change rapidly during iteration. A common misconception is that you must keep the Playable Director on the same object as animated actors — it is usually better on a manager object to centralize control, and you bind actors to tracks inside the Timeline. By following these steps you create a clean, reusable pattern: asset in Project, director on a manager object, and tracks bound to targets, making collaboration and iteration straightforward.

keyIdea.title: Setup pattern
keyIdea.text: Create the Timeline Asset in the Project, add a Playable Director on a manager GameObject, then open the Timeline window to author tracks.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Create Asset & Director
Step-by-step
  1. Create Timeline Asset in Project (right-click → Create → Timeline)
  2. Create an empty GameObject in the scene and name it (e.g., IntroSequenceManager)
  3. Add a Playable Director component to that GameObject
  4. Drag the Timeline Asset into the Playable field
  5. Open Window → Sequencing → Timeline to author tracks
Tip: store Timeline Assets in a dedicated folder and add to version control early.
Visual checklist
Timeline Asset
A file in your Project that holds tracks and clips.
Playable Director
Attaches to an empty GameObject and plays the asset in-scene.
Manager Pattern
Keep the director on a manager object to centralize playback and triggers.
Key Takeaway

A Timeline Asset plus Playable Director is the canonical pattern for reusable cinematic sequences in Unity.

screens.title: Track types and their roles
screens.subtitle: Understand Animation, Activation, Audio, and Control tracks

narration.text: Timeline is built from horizontal lanes called tracks. Each track type has a specific role: Animation Tracks drive transform and property keyframes or play animation clips directly; Activation Tracks toggle GameObject active states at precise moments, perfect for revealing or hiding props; Audio Tracks play sounds and music and can be snapped to beats; Control Tracks can call other Playable Directors, trigger particle systems, or play custom playable assets, making them valuable for nested sequences. When you add a track you must bind a target GameObject by dragging it to the track header. Without binding the track will control nothing — a frequent oversight. Use Animation Tracks for simple clip playback or quick keyframe recording; use Animator (Animator Track) when you need to drive the Animator Controller and maintain root motion and parameter-driven state machines. Use Activation Tracks to manage visibility and life-cycle of scene objects, especially when starting objects disabled in the Hierarchy. Control Tracks are ideal for orchestrating nested timelines or particle systems so you can compose large sequences from smaller, versioned parts. Understanding these roles helps you choose the right lane to author predictable, maintainable cinematic behavior.

keyIdea.title: Track roles
keyIdea.text: Choose tracks by role: Animation (clips/keyframes), Activation (enable/disable), Audio (play sound), Control (nested or custom playables).

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Track Types
Track quick-reference
Animation Track
Play clips or record keyframes; binds to a GameObject to control its properties.
Activation Track
Enable or disable objects at specific times — useful for reveals and lifecycle control.
Audio Track
Place and snap audio clips to hits and beats for precise sound design.
Control Track
Control nested timelines, particle systems, or custom playable assets for composition.
Binding and behavior
  • Always drag the target GameObject onto the track header to bind controls.
  • Animation Tracks override transforms directly; use Animator/Animator Track if you need root motion or state machine control.
  • Control Tracks are perfect for nesting sequences so that large scenes remain modular.
Key Takeaway

Pick the track that matches the asset you need to control: visibility, clip playback, audio timing, or nested composition.

screens.title: Animation Track: clips, recording, and blending
screens.subtitle: How to place clips, record keyframes, and create blends

narration.text: Animation Tracks are your primary tool for moving objects and characters in a Timeline sequence. You can drag existing animation clips from the Project directly onto the track, creating Animation Clip Playables that play at the specified time and length. When clips overlap, Timeline blends them to create smooth transitions — a useful way to crossfade from 'Idle' to 'Walk'. Alternatively, select the bound GameObject and press the red record button in the Timeline window to capture keyframes in the scene, which is handy for animating camera pans or prop interactions without switching to the Animation window. When recording, move the playhead and adjust transforms; Timeline records those values as keyframes. Remember that Animation Tracks tend to directly control transforms. If your character requires root motion driven by the Animator Controller, prefer an Animator Track so the Animator can apply root motion and parameter logic. A common issue is misaligned clip lengths or accidental looping; check clip speed, start/end times, and loop settings. The example workflow: drag a 'Walk' clip onto a character's Animation Track, shorten the clip to match the entrance, and overlap slightly with a previous 'Idle' clip to let Timeline blend them smoothly.

keyIdea.title: Animation Track
keyIdea.text: Use Animation Tracks for clip playback and keyframe recording; overlap clips to blend transitions, or use Animator Tracks for root motion.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Animation Track
How to use clips
Drag animation clips to the track to create playables. Set start and end times, adjust speed, and use overlap to blend between clips automatically.
Recording
Select the bound GameObject and click the record button to key transforms over time. Ideal for camera pans and prop interactions.
Practical example
Place an 'Idle' clip, then drag a 'Walk' clip to start when the character enters. Overlap them slightly to let Timeline blend the transition.
Watch clip speed and loop settings to avoid sliding or unexpected repeats.
Key Takeaway

Animation Tracks are for clip placement and keyframe recording; use Animator Tracks when you need Animator-driven root motion and state behavior.

screens.title: Animation Track vs Animator Track
screens.subtitle: When to use direct clips and when to drive the Animator Controller

narration.text: Animation Tracks and Animator Tracks both control animated behavior but in different ways. An Animation Track plays animation clips or records keyframes and often directly manipulates the GameObject's transform. This is fast for simple object motion or camera recording. The Animator Track, by contrast, drives the character's Animator Controller and respects the Animator's parameter logic and root motion so animations that move the character through world space behave consistently. Consider a 'Jump' clip that contains root motion: placing it on an Animation Track may cause foot sliding because Timeline will directly set the transform instead of letting the Animator apply root motion. The remedy is to use an Animator Track bound to the character; Timeline will then interact with the Animator Controller and allow root motion and state transitions to drive movement properly. A misconception is thinking direct clips always preserve complex character behavior — they do not. Use direct Animation Tracks for props, cameras, and simple object animations; use Animator Tracks whenever an Animator Controller, root motion, or parameter-driven state changes are required. This distinction prevents motion artifacts and preserves animator-driven behavior in cinematic sequences.

keyIdea.title: Comparison
keyIdea.text: Animation Track: direct clips and keyframes. Animator Track: drives Animator Controller, preserves root motion and state-driven behavior.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Animation vs Animator
Side-by-side
Animation Track
Best for cameras, props, and direct clip placement. Controls transforms directly.
Animator Track
Best for characters that rely on Animator Controller logic and root motion.
Practical guidance
  • Use Animation Tracks for camera pans and simple clip sequencing.
  • Use Animator Tracks when you need root motion or parameter-driven transitions.
  • Test movement in-play to check for sliding and adjust by switching track type if needed.
Common Mistake

Placing root-motion clips on Animation Tracks can cause sliding. Prefer Animator Track for root motion.

screens.title: Adding clips and binding GameObjects
screens.subtitle: How binding works and why it matters for control

narration.text: Adding content to a track is straightforward but binding is the step that makes the track functional. To add clips, drag an animation or audio clip from the Project window onto the desired track. For Animation Tracks, dropping a clip creates an Animation Clip Playable at that time position. For Audio Tracks, dropping a sound clip places an audio playable you can trim and snap. After adding clips, bind the target GameObject by dragging it from the Hierarchy onto the track header. Without binding the track has no reference to which object to control and nothing will happen during playback. A practical scenario: you add a 'Walk' clip to a character's Animation Track, but if you forget to bind the character the clip will sit there inert — the Timeline cannot find the target to animate. Another detail is clip trimming and speed adjustments: you can shorten a clip, change its playback speed, or enable looping in the clip properties to match your cinematic timing. As you populate tracks, use snapping and the playhead to precisely align the start of clips with activation events and audio cues so all elements trigger cohesively.

keyIdea.title: Binding matters
keyIdea.text: Drag target GameObjects onto track headers to bind; clips without bindings have no effect during playback.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Add & Bind
Actions
  • Drag clip from Project onto a track to create a playable.
  • Trim or change clip speed to match timing.
  • Drag the Hierarchy GameObject onto the track header to bind it.
Tip: bind before recording keyframes so Timeline knows where to store property changes.
Example scenario
Add an Activation Track for the character, bind the character GameObject, then add an Animation Track and drag the Walk clip onto it. Ensure the character is initially disabled in the Hierarchy so the Activation Track reveals it at the correct time.
Common Mistake

Placing clips without binding the GameObject — the clip will not affect any scene object until bound.

screens.title: Camera recording and animating field of view
screens.subtitle: Record transforms and tweak FOV for cinematic reveals

narration.text: Animating the camera in Timeline is a quick way to create cinematic reveals and controlled pans without complex scripting. Start by creating a Camera GameObject for the shot and add an Animation Track bound to that camera. Click the red record button in the Timeline window to begin recording; scrub the playhead and move the camera to capture position and rotation keyframes over time. You can also key the camera's field of view to create a subtle zoom or dramatic focus shift. When recording, move the camera incrementally and stop recording when the motion feels natural; Timeline stores each adjustment as a keyframe. A concrete example: record a slow dolly backward while slightly narrowing the FOV as the character comes into frame to increase perceived distance and drama. Keep an eye on interpolation — adjust tangents or add intermediate keyframes to avoid abrupt motion. A common misconception is overusing wide FOV changes; small FOV adjustments are usually more cinematic. Practice by creating a short camera pan that syncs with a character's entrance to feel the difference recording makes versus manual placement of static keyframes.

keyIdea.title: Camera tips
keyIdea.text: Record camera position, rotation, and FOV on an Animation Track to create smooth pans and reveal shots that sync with other timeline events.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Camera Recording
Recording workflow
  1. Create a Camera GameObject and add an Animation Track bound to it.
  2. Click the record button and move the playhead while adjusting camera transforms.
  3. Key FOV changes for subtle zooms to emphasize storytelling beats.
Tip: use small FOV adjustments and smooth tangents to avoid jarring perspective shifts.
Example
Record a slow dolly out and slightly narrow FOV as the character walks in to heighten drama and reveal context.
Key Takeaway

Recording camera keyframes in Timeline provides fine-grained, editable motion that easily syncs with other tracks.

screens.title: Synchronizing audio and visual beats
screens.subtitle: Using Audio Tracks and snapping to align cues

narration.text: Audio is a powerful tool for guiding attention and emotional response. In Timeline, Audio Tracks let you place music, sound effects, and dialogue and snap them to beats and visual events. Drag an audio clip onto an Audio Track, then use the timeline's snapping tools and playhead to align the start of the clip with an animation or activation event. Trim the clip length and adjust volume or loop settings as needed. A practical routine is to place a dramatic music hit at the exact frame when a character becomes visible and then start a walk clip slightly after to create forward momentum. Remember to preview in Play mode because audio fades and spatial settings may differ from the editor preview. A common misconception is thinking Audio Tracks alone control spatialization; you should ensure audio source settings and mixer configuration match your intended result. For small sequences, adjust timing by nudging clips left or right, and use fade-in/out settings to smooth transitions. The goal is precise alignment so visual reveals and audio hits reinforce one another. Synchronizing audio and visual beats means place and snap audio clips on audio tracks to align sound cues with animation and activation events for stronger emotional impact.. In practical terms, using audio tracks and snapping to align cues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Audio sync
keyIdea.text: Place and snap audio clips on Audio Tracks to align sound cues with animation and activation events for stronger emotional impact.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Audio & Sync
Steps to sync
  • Drag an audio clip onto an Audio Track.
  • Use snapping and the playhead to align the clip with a visual event.
  • Trim and set fades to smooth transitions between cues.
Preview in Play mode to confirm spatialization and mixer effects.
Example
Place a music swell at the exact frame of a character reveal and start the walk animation just after, creating an audio-visual cue pair.
Pro Tip

Use subtle fades to blend audio clips seamlessly when shifting between cues or when looping background music.

screens.title: Control Tracks and nested timelines
screens.subtitle: Compose larger sequences from smaller Timeline Assets

narration.text: Control Tracks are essential when your cinematic grows beyond a single sequence. They let you call nested Timeline Assets or trigger particle systems and other playable assets from a parent timeline, which keeps large sequences modular and maintainable. The workflow is to create smaller Timeline Assets for reusable moments — for example, a short character entrance animation or a particle flourish — and then add a Control Track in the master Timeline to play those nested assets at specific times. This approach gives you versioned components that multiple directors can reuse, and it prevents a single Timeline from becoming unwieldy. A concrete scenario: build a short 'sparkle' Timeline asset for a treasure reveal, then from the main chest Timeline add a Control Track bound to the particle system and reference the sparkle Timeline as a nested playable so it triggers exactly when the chest opens. A common mistake is leaving multiple Playable Directors active simultaneously without clear ownership; ensure only the intended Director plays the master timeline or control track to avoid conflicts. The key benefit is modularity — small, testable sequences composed together form complex cinematics that are easier to share and update.

keyIdea.title: Control & nesting
keyIdea.text: Use Control Tracks to trigger nested Timeline Assets and playables, keeping large sequences modular and reusable.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Control Tracks
Why nest timelines
Nesting keeps sequences modular. Create small Timeline Assets for reusable moments and trigger them from a master Timeline using a Control Track.
Benefit: smaller assets are easier to version, test, and update independently.
Example
Create a 'sparkle' Timeline for a particle effect and trigger it from the chest Timeline using a Control Track when the chest opens.
Key Takeaway

Control Tracks let you compose sequences from smaller, reusable Timeline Assets to keep cinematic projects manageable.

screens.title: Common mistakes and best practices
screens.subtitle: Avoid binding errors, director conflicts, and preserve iterative workflows

narration.text: When authoring timelines, several common mistakes can cause unexpected behavior. First, forgetting to bind GameObjects to tracks is the most frequent problem — a clip without a bound target controls nothing. Second, enabling multiple Playable Directors at once can create conflicts if they attempt to control the same objects simultaneously; keep one Director authoritative for a sequence or design clear handoffs. Third, placing root-motion animations on Animation Tracks instead of Animator Tracks can lead to sliding or incorrect movement — use Animator Tracks for animator-driven root motion. For best practices, keep Timeline Assets small and modular, use Control Tracks to nest sequences, and commit assets to version control to preserve iterative changes. Regularly save Timeline Assets after edits, and preview sequences frequently in Play mode to catch differences between editor playback and runtime audio or spatialization. For triggers, prefer using Playable Director playback calls or event-driven scripts that explicitly start the intended timeline rather than relying on multiple Directors toggling themselves. The practical outcome: reliable, maintainable cinematic systems that are easy to update and collaborate on with other artists and designers.

keyIdea.title: Best practices
keyIdea.text: Bind targets, avoid concurrent Directors, use Animator Tracks for root motion, modularize with nested timelines, and use version control.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Mistakes & Practices
Common mistakes
  • Not binding GameObjects to tracks so clips have no effect.
  • Multiple Playable Directors acting on the same objects simultaneously.
  • Using Animation Tracks for root-motion clips when Animator Tracks are required.
Best practices
Modularize with small Timeline Assets, nest with Control Tracks, save and commit Timeline Assets regularly, and test playback in Play mode.
Key Takeaway

Adopt a modular, versioned workflow and resolve director ownership to produce predictable cinematic sequences.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Here are the essential terms and concepts to retain. Timeline is Unity's non-linear sequencer used to arrange animations, audio, and events. A Timeline Asset stores sequence data and is played in-scene by a Playable Director on a manager GameObject. Tracks are lanes for specific types of control: Animation Tracks for clip playback and keyframes, Activation Tracks for enabling and disabling GameObjects, Audio Tracks for sound cues, and Control Tracks for nesting other playable assets. Binding a GameObject to a track is required so the track knows what to control. Use Animator Tracks when an Animator Controller or root motion must drive character movement to avoid sliding. Nest smaller Timeline Assets with Control Tracks to keep large sequences modular. Common pitfalls include forgetting to bind targets, running multiple Playable Directors on the same objects, and misplacing root-motion clips. Keep Timeline Assets versioned, test frequently in Play mode, and iterate visually to align audio and visuals precisely. These practices help you build reliable, maintainable cinematics that can be shared and refined across a team.

Timeline
A non-linear editor that sequences tracks and clips to build cinematics.
Playable Director
Component that references and plays a Timeline Asset in a scene.
Tracks
Animation, Activation, Audio, Control — lanes that drive different elements over time.
Takeaway

Use the right track type, bind targets, and prefer Animator Tracks for root motion. Modularize with nested timelines and version Timeline Assets to keep work stable.

narration.text: A final compact review: always bind your GameObjects to tracks so actions have targets. Remember the difference between Animation and Animator Tracks — one directly manipulates transforms while the other interacts with an Animator Controller and preserves root motion. Use Activation Tracks to toggle GameObjects on and off at specific times and Audio Tracks to align sound with visual cues. When sequences grow complex, use Control Tracks to nest smaller Timeline Assets and keep your cinematic modular. Finally, adopt source control habits for Timeline Assets and preview sequences regularly in Play mode to catch runtime differences. These small habits prevent common errors and make your cinematic work easier to share and iterate on with other artists and designers. What to Remember means bind targets, choose correct track types, nest with control tracks, and use version control and play mode previews for reliability.. Bind Targets
Tracks control bound GameObjects; ensure binding is done after adding a track.
Choose Track Type
Animation for clips, Animator for root motion, Activation for visibility, Audio for cues.
Nest & Version
Use Control Tracks to nest and commit Timeline Assets to version control for safe iteration.
Final Note

Treat Timeline as a visual hub for timing. Bind, choose the correct track, nest modular assets, and test early to build reliable cinematics.

ai_generation_note: Create a 15-minute interactive lab video. Start with a simple scene and a pre-animated character (with an Animator Controller). Guide the learner through creating a Timeline Asset and a Playable Director. Demonstrate adding an Activation Track for the character (initially hidden) and an Animation Track for the character. Show how to drag a "Walk" animation clip onto the Animation Track and adjust its timing. Then, add an Audio Track and drag a background music clip onto it. Finally, create a new Camera, add an Animation Track for it, and demonstrate recording keyframes to create a simple camera pan that reveals the walking character. End with a mini-quiz asking about the purpose of Activation Tracks and the difference between Animation and Animator Tracks in Timeline.
